item.title: Expert hails China-S.Korea civil exchanges as Chinese visitors drive 21.3% surge in Jan-Jul
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-26
Expert hails China-S.Korea civil exchanges as Chinese visitors drive 21.3% surge in Jan-Jul Tourists are seen around the Namsan Seoul Tower in Seoul, South Korea, July, 18, 2026. (Photo by Jun Hyosang/Xinhua) A Chinese expert hailed the closer people-to-people exchanges between China and South Korea on Tuesday, as South Korea recorded an increase of 21.3 percent in foreign visitor arrivals during the first seven months this year, with the Chinese mainland topping the list. The tourism boom helps enhance mutual understanding, stimulate consumption and injects more positive, pragmatic momentum into bilateral relations, analysts said. The Yonhap News Agency reported on Tuesday that from January to July, cumulative foreign visitor arrivals to South Korea rose to 12.8 million. By source market, the Chinese mainland topped the list with 3.99 million, followed by Japan with 2.28 million. In July alone, foreign visitor arrivals to South Korea increased 20.8 percent, and the Chinese mainland again ranked the first. Compared with the same month in 2019, arrivals from the Chinese mainland and Japan rose 49.6 percent and 20.2 percent respectively, said the report. "The figures highlighted the key role of Chinese visitors and confirmed the robust recovery of the China-South Korea tourism market," Lü Chao, a research fellow on North Korea with the Liaoning Academy of Social Sciences, told the Global Times on Tuesday. Lü noted that bilateral relations have gradually warmed through pragmatic exchanges, with tourism serving as the most direct "thermometer." "South Korea launched a visa-free trial for Chinese group tourists starting in September 2025, along with stepping up the expansion of flight frequencies and improving service management, further unlocking two-way demand," the expert said. Jeju Air saw its passenger traffic increase by nearly 40 percent year-on-year during the first seven months of this year on routes between the two countries, Yonhap reported. From January to July, seat capacity on Jeju Air's South Korea-China routes grew by 26.8 percent year-on-year to 494,300 seats, while passenger traffic rose by 37.4 percent year-on-year to 427,300 travelers, and the load factor climbed 6.6 percentage points to 86.4 percent, according to Yonhap. At the same time, the number of South Korean visitors to China has also grown significantly following China's implementation and extension of visa-free policies for South Korean citizens. ModeTour, a leading South Korean travel operator, posted explosive growth in China-related reservations. Its summer travel bookings to China soared 105 percent year-on-year, according to a press release. The agency attributed the travel boom to short-haul flights, affordable on-site spending, visa-free entry policies and enlarged airline capacity. Data from ModeTour showed that Changbai Mountain in Northeast China's Jilin Province accounted for 41 percent of its China summer packages, followed by Zhangjiajie in Central China's Hunan at 21 percent, and Qingdao, East China's Shandong, at 8 percent. Lü noted that due to Japan's erroneous remarks on Taiwan, which have strained China-Japan relations, many Chinese tourists have abandoned their plans to visit Japan, making South Korea a preferred choice. "The travel boom between the two neighboring countries helps enhance mutual understanding, stimulate consumption and injects more positive, pragmatic people-to-people momentum into bilateral relations. With mutual visa facilitation, denser flight networks and warmer bilateral ties, exchanges are expected to maintain strong growth, further deepening friendship and practical cooperation between the two neighboring countries," Lü said. Monday marked the 34th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations between China and South Korea. Lin Jian, a spokesperson of China's Foreign Ministry, told a press conference on Monday that "Over the past 34 years, our two countries, as friendly neighbors, have become inseparable strategic cooperative partners with all-round and rapid growth in political cooperation, economy and trade, people-to-people and cultural exchanges." The development of bilateral relations is in keeping with the trend of the times, serves the shared interests of both countries, and contributes to regional peace and development, Lin said, noting that China has always placed South Korea high on its agenda for neighborhood diplomacy and stands ready to work with the South Korean side to implement the common understandings reached by the two heads of state, bring the bilateral strategic cooperative partnership to new heights, and deliver more benefits to the two peoples. item.title: 'Economic D-Day'? The US has picked wrong script for sanctioning Iran
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-26
'Economic D-Day'? The US has picked wrong script for sanctioning Iran Comparing an illegal unilateral sanctions campaign with no basis in international law and no authorization from the UN Security Council to the allied landing in Normandy, one of the defining battles of the anti-fascist war, is an absurd analogy. Forcing a stalled military conflict into the arena of economic confrontation only underscores how few cards the US has left to play. On Monday local time, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced a new round of sanctions against Iran under a plan dubbed "operation economic outcast." What is particularly bizarre is the name he gave the campaign: "economic D-Day." Comparing an illegal unilateral sanctions campaign with no basis in international law and no authorization from the UN Security Council to the allied landing in Normandy, one of the defining battles of the anti-fascist war, is an absurd analogy. The substance of the campaign is to extend sanctions to the countries that do business with Iran, effectively seeking to "sever every economic lifeline" available to Tehran. International opinion generally sees this more as a US "remedial measure" after military means failed to deliver results. Bloomberg economics analysts described that it left "major questions outstanding." Forcing a stalled military conflict into the arena of economic confrontation only underscores how few cards the US has left to play. The US has steadily tightened sanctions on Iran since 1979, yet has never managed to force Tehran to submit. Now Washington is serving up the same old recipe with a familiar taste, merely under the new label of an "operation economic outcast" campaign. Although Iran's average daily oil exports have plunged from around 2 million barrels before the war to approximately 287,000 barrels in August, Tehran still holds the key strategic leverage of the Strait of Hormuz and has accumulated extensive experience in coping with sanctions for a long time. If nearly 50 years of sanctions failed to achieve the goal, can simply giving them a "D-Day" label finally make them work? Through secondary sanctions, the US is not merely deciding "who it will do business with," but attempting to dictate to other countries around the world "who they can do business with." In doing so, Washington is opening multiple fronts at once: waging an economic war against Iran while simultaneously fighting sanctions battles with China, India, Turkey and even its European allies. Bessent has even threatened that countries that fail to cooperate could be excluded from the dollar system. It is a blatant weaponization of the dollar, turning the global financial system into a tool of unilateral punishment. When one country can arbitrarily cut off another country's economic lifelines at will, the foundations of the international economic and trade system are undermined, ultimately eroding confidence in the dollar's global credibility. Economic sanctions often trigger unintended chain reactions. The international oil prices have risen by over 50 percent so far this year. Further tightening restrictions on Iran's oil exports would only push oil prices higher and intensify inflationary pressures, casting an even darker shadow over an already fragile global economic recovery. The Strait of Hormuz is one of the world's most important energy chokepoints, and any disruption there could trigger sharp volatility in global energy markets. When economic measures are used as instruments of war, the risks won't remain within the boundaries envisioned by the US. They will spread and spill over, ultimately leaving everyone to foot the bill. The most urgent task now is not to escalate confrontation, but to de-escalate the situation. Dialogue and negotiations are the only right path toward resolving the US-Iran War and the Iranian nuclear issue, and this is a broad consensus in the international community. Unilateral sanctions and threats of force will not help resolve the problem; instead, they will exacerbate tensions and narrow the space for diplomacy. The US should seriously reflect on the gains and losses of its policy toward Iran, rather than blindly pressing ahead down a path that has already been proven to be a dead end. The so-called "operation economic outcast" is itself a reflection of the predicament facing US policy. Even Washington may have little confidence in how effective the new sanctions will be. More importantly, today's world is no longer one in which a single country can unilaterally determine the fate of other countries. Global multipolarity is an irreversible historical trend, and countries making independent choices based on their own national interests is simply a basic fact of international relations. It should be noted that some US media outlets have deliberately sought to turn attention toward China, attempting to create a narrative that the success or failure of the campaign depends on whether China cooperates. The possibility that Washington could use the regional conflict to exert additional economic pressure on China warrants vigilance. China's cooperation with Iran has always been conducted within the framework of international law and should not be disrupted or undermined. China is not a party to US military actions against Iran or the Iranian nuclear issue, and should certainly not be held responsible for the failure of US policy. Some people in the US should focus on how to build "a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability," rather than constantly seeking to create turmoil in bilateral relations. In May this year, China's Ministry of Commerce, for the first time, issued a blocking ban under the rules on countering foreign states' unlawful extraterritorial jurisdiction measures, explicitly prohibiting any recognition, enforcement or compliance with US sanctions imposed on five Chinese companies on the grounds of their alleged involvement in Iranian petroleum transactions. China has a comprehensive range of legal and policy tools at its disposal and will take all necessary measures to firmly safeguard its legitimate rights and interests. Any attempt to force China to submit through sanctions and pressure will not succeed. Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. All Rights Reserved.

item.title: China mulls road safety law revisions, law against cross-border corruption
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-26
China mulls road safety law revisions, law against cross-border corruption Zhao Leji, chairman of the National People's Congress (NPC) Standing Committee, presides over the first plenary meeting of the 24th session of the 14th NPC Standing Committee at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing, capital of China, Aug. 25, 2026. (Xinhua/Pang Xinglei) BEIJING, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- Chinese lawmakers convened on Tuesday to review a raft of bills, including draft revisions to the Road Traffic Safety Law, a draft law on combating cross-border corruption and a draft healthcare security law. The bills were submitted for deliberation at the 24th session of the Standing Committee of the 14th National People's Congress (NPC), the country's top legislature. Zhao Leji, chairman of the NPC Standing Committee, presided over the first plenary meeting of the session. In the meeting, lawmakers deliberated a draft healthcare security law. Submitted for a third reading, the draft includes provisions on long-term care insurance, aiming to further protect the rights and interests of insured people. A draft law on farmland protection and quality improvement was submitted for its third reading, adding provisions on talent cultivation and strengthening oversight of funds for high-standard farmland development. Lawmakers also reviewed a revised draft of the Agriculture Law, which improves support for agricultural and rural economic development, enhances protection for farmers' rights and interests, and strengthens rural development and governance. A draft revision to the National Defense Mobilization Law was submitted for its second reading. The revisions clarify the concept of national defense mobilization and rules on the collection, use and security management of relevant data. Lawmakers reviewed a draft amendment to the lawyers law that improves the provisions to boost foreign-related legal services. A revised draft of the Enterprise Bankruptcy Law, submitted for its second reading, refines rules on the bankruptcy of individual debtors bearing joint and several liability, improves the reorganization system, and adjusts the priority order for distributions from the bankruptcy estate. Also under review was a revised draft of the banking supervision and regulation law, which introduces classified and tiered supervision of banking institutions, improves the system for protecting banking consumers' rights and interests, and adds a separate chapter on risk resolution. Lawmakers also reviewed a revised draft of the Water Law. The second-reading draft strengthens provisions on the protection of water resources and water ecology, national water network development, and water conservation and recycling. Draft revisions to the Road Traffic Safety Law were submitted for review, seeking to improve the road traffic safety management system and strengthen the legal framework for maintaining traffic order. The draft includes a dedicated chapter on autonomous vehicles. A draft law on combating cross-border corruption was submitted for the first reading, aiming to prevent and punish transnational corruption, deepen international cooperation and safeguard national sovereignty, security, and development interests. Lawmakers also heard a series of reports, including a report on the implementation of the 2026 plan for national economic and social development, a report on budget execution, a report on government debt management in 2025, and a supervisory research report on government debt management in 2025. A report on improving the quality of cultural products and services and a report on efforts to consolidate and expand achievements in poverty alleviation and advance all-around rural revitalization were also on the agenda of the lawmakers. Lawmakers also deliberated an extradition treaty between China and Hungary, a deputy qualification report and personnel-related bills. Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. All Rights Reserved.

item.title: China striving to ensure good start to 15th Five-Year Plan period: official
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-26
China striving to ensure good start to 15th Five-Year Plan period: official BEIJING, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- China is working to promote sustained economic development toward new and higher-quality growth with positive momentum, and striving to ensure a sound start to the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), said Wang Changlin, deputy head of the National Development and Reform Commission, on Tuesday. Entrusted by the State Council, Wang made the remarks when presenting a report on the implementation of the national economic and social development plan since the start of this year to the ongoing session of the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress, the country's top legislature. Wang said China's gross domestic product (GDP) grew 4.7 percent year on year in the first half of 2026, with economic output increasing by 3.6 trillion yuan (530.57 billion U.S. dollars), marking the largest increase in five years for this period. Indicators including economic growth, employment, prices and foreign trade were in line with expectations, while consumption and residents' income maintained steady growth. China's economy has a stable foundation, many advantages, strong resilience and great potential. The underlying support conditions and the fundamental trend of long-term sound development remain unchanged, Wang noted. To do a good job in economic work in the second half of the year, Wang said China should adhere to the general principle of pursuing progress while ensuring stability, continue to deepen reform and opening up, and accelerate the transition from old growth drivers to new ones. China should effectively implement a more proactive fiscal policy and an appropriately accommodative monetary policy, make full use of existing policy measures, and introduce pragmatic and effective incremental policies in a timely manner, Wang added. Efforts should also be made to step up counter-cyclical adjustments, further expand domestic demand and optimize supply, and effectively safeguard and improve people's livelihoods, Wang said. item.title: China warns against unilateral sanctions after U.S. vows "economic asphyxiation" of Iran
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-26
China warns against unilateral sanctions after U.S. vows "economic asphyxiation" of Iran BEIJING, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- China has made clear on multiple occasions that it firmly opposes illegal unilateral sanctions that have no basis in international law and are not authorized by the UN Security Council, Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Lin Jian said on Tuesday. Lin made the remarks at a regular news briefing when asked to comment on media reports that U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday laid out plans for the "economic asphyxiation" of Iran, expanding Washington's secondary sanctions threats and warning of dire consequences for countries that do not join the campaign. Economic warfare and maximum pressure do not help solve problems. Instead, they only escalate tensions and conflicts, create spillover risks, disrupt the global economic and financial order, and undermine the legitimate rights and interests of other countries, Lin said. The pressing priority now is to de-escalate the situation and return to the track of dialogue and negotiation as soon as possible, he added. China's cooperation with Iran is always conducted within the framework of international law and should not be disrupted or undermined, Lin said. China is closely following relevant developments and will take all necessary measures to resolutely safeguard its legitimate rights and interests, he noted. Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. All Rights Reserved.

item.title: Forest treasures become art in N China's Inner Mongolia
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-26
Forest treasures become art in N China's Inner Mongolia With her nose brushing against the dense pine needles, Fu Lihong seems to catch a glimpse of the vast pine forests before her. Each stroke in these artworks is not painted, but in fact created by carefully arranging pine needles, pine cones, and dried bark collected from the Greater Khingan Mountains, north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region. As a representative inheritor of the intangible cultural heritage of Mengxiaosong pine cone painting, Fu has a deep bond with the forest. Photo shows pine cone paintings created by Fu Lihong displayed at the forest culture art museum she founded. (People's Daily Online/Liu Yilin) Fu's father was a forestry worker. As a child, she often followed her father into the forest, where pine nuts were her favorite snack. Those childhood memories of running through the woods later became the inspiration for her creations. Since the 1950s, Arxan has carried out large-scale afforestation efforts. Fu's father was among those who planted trees at the time. By 1992, the preserved area of Arxan's artificial forests had reached 1 million mu (about 66,667 hectares). Materials used for making pine cone paintings are displayed at the art museum. (People's Daily Online/Liu Yilin) Trees planted by previous generations now provide shade for those who follow. What others see as withered branches and fallen leaves have become treasures in Fu's hands. Materials used for making pine cone paintings are displayed at the art museum. (People's Daily Online/Zhang Liyang) Over three years, Fu traveled through the forest across all four seasons, collecting large quantities of pine cones and leaves. After gathering nearly 1 million pine needles, she created a series of one-of-a-kind artworks. In 2021, Fu founded the Mengxiaosong Forest Culture Art Museum, the only museum in Inner Mongolia dedicated to pine tree culture. Photo shows pine cone creative cultural products displayed at the art museum. (People's Daily Online/Liu Yilin) The museum is more than just an exhibition space: Fu developed an art course which takes children into the forest to learn about plants in the Greater Khingan Mountains before returning to the museum to create their own pine cone paintings. In 2024, the course was recognized as an outstanding study-tour program in Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region. The museum has also created jobs for local residents. Fu hires forestry workers with spare time to collect pine cones and pine needles, which are then used in her creations. She is also training inheritors of the intangible cultural heritage craft, helping more people master the technique. An art course, developed by Fu Lihong, which takes children into the forest to learn about plants in the Greater Khingan Mountains, is an outstanding study tour program in Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region. (People's Daily Online/Liu Yilin) Photo shows pine cone creative cultural products displayed at the art museum. (People's Daily Online/Liu Yilin) Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. item.title: China reports steady consolidation of poverty alleviation gains
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-26
China reports steady consolidation of poverty alleviation gains A drone photo taken on May 15, 2026 shows a view of the tea gardens in Luxi Village of Jingde County, Xuancheng City, east China's Anhui Province. (Xinhua/Zhou Mu) BEIJING, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- China's poverty alleviation outcomes have been steadily consolidated and expanded, with rural per capita income showing a stable rise, a State Council report has revealed. The report on consolidating poverty alleviation achievements and advancing rural revitalization was submitted for deliberation at the ongoing session of the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress, the country's top legislature, which opened on Tuesday. According to the report, the per capita disposable income of rural residents in counties that have been removed from the poverty list rose from 12,588 yuan (about 1,855 U.S. dollars) in 2020 to 18,627 yuan in 2025, achieving average annual growth of 8.2 percent. It also noted marked improvements in rural infrastructure and public services, and a narrowing development gap compared with other regions. Industrial and employment assistance have been stepped up, and efforts have been made to stabilize jobs for those who have been lifted out of poverty. The number of such people with jobs has exceeded 32 million, the report said. The report also acknowledged persistent challenges, including long-term risks of relapse into poverty and weak development foundations in less-developed areas. Looking ahead, regular assistance will be integrated into the overall rural revitalization strategy, with people at risk of falling back into poverty and underdeveloped regions remaining as the primary targets of assistance. The approach will combine development-oriented support with a sound social security system to safeguard basic livelihoods, the report said. Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. All Rights Reserved.

item.title: A Maowusu reunion rooted in American's kindness, forged by Chinese farmer's grit
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-25
Feature: A Maowusu reunion rooted in American's kindness, forged by Chinese farmer's grit Yin Yuzhen (L), Bai Wanxiang (R) and Ronald Sakolsky pose for a photo with a tree they once planted together in the Maowusu Sandy Land in north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, Aug. 24, 2026. Retired U.S. teacher Ronald Sakolsky revisited the Maowusu Sandy Land on Monday and planted sapling with his friend Yin Yuzhen, a national model worker who has been planting trees here for four decades, as well as Yin's husband Bai Wanxiang. (Xinhua/Lian Zhen) HOHHOT, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- For more than a quarter of a century, a retired American teacher and a Chinese woman fighting desertification have lived on opposite sides of the Pacific, bound together by old photos, a newspaper and a forest. On Sunday, they finally met again, face to face. As Ronald Sakolsky descended an escalator at an airport in Ordos, north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, he wiped tears from his eyes with his right hand while clutching a bouquet in his left. At the bottom stood Yin Yuzhen, a woman who has spent over four decades wringing green life from the Maowusu, the fourth-largest sandy area in China. The short ride down the escalator was the last stretch before their long-awaited embrace, 26 years after their first in-person meeting. Their friendship began in 1999, when Sakolsky taught English at a school in central China's Henan Province -- more than 11,000 kilometers from his home in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, under a teachers' exchange program between the two countries. One ordinary evening, a television program caught his eye. On the screen was Yin, planting trees to help hold back the advancing sands of the Maowusu sandy land. Stretching across parts of Inner Mongolia, Shaanxi and Ningxia, the Maowusu has been one of the front lines in China's fight against desertification in the north: an effort launched in 1978 and slated to continue through 2050. But for Yin, the fight against the sand was not an abstract national effort. In those years, a night of strong winds could leave the doorway of their dugout sealed by sand. There was grit in the food, dirt in the water, and little else in sight but miles of shifting yellow stretching in every direction. By 1999, Yin had planted trees across some 30,000 mu (about 2,000 hectares) of barren land -- an area equivalent to around 2,800 standard soccer pitches. "I was so touched that I started to cry," Sakolsky recalled, thinking back to that evening. "I honestly cannot tell you why. Something just happened to me. I just felt like I needed to help." Over the next two months, he contacted more than a dozen organizations across the United States. A Boston-based charity agreed to provide a grant of 5,000 U.S. dollars. At the time, the donation was a staggering sum for Yin -- enough to build a house, cover the costs of raising her children, and give her family a very different life. Yet, Yin spent it all on saplings, keeping only a single banknote as a memento. In May 2000, Sakolsky took a train from Luoyang, Henan, and then switched to another vehicle, jolting all the way into the sandy land to see the saplings with his own eyes. He later described the landscape as desolate: "No roads, no trees, no houses. We were just driving over one dune after another." Then he spotted Yin. "She popped out of a hole," Sakolsky said. The two couldn't speak each other's language, and they relied entirely on gestures and smiles to communicate. Yin showed Sakolsky how to plant. To Sakolsky, the saplings looked so fragile that he thought they might never grow much higher than his knees. Deep down, he could not see how this patch of sand could ever become a forest. He told her so plainly: "This is impossible." That night, Yin and her husband invited him to their home for dinner, and made him a steaming bowl of noodles. "Delicious," Sakolsky recalled. Sakolsky went home months later, and they lost touch. Across the Pacific, he kept telling his students about the Chinese woman who was trying to turn a desert green. In China, whenever Yin met an American, she would pull out an old photograph of Sakolsky and ask if they knew how she could get in touch with him. RECONNECTED ONLINE Year after year, her search went nowhere, until a video and a social media post achieved what years of searching had not. In May this year, Yin stood before the forest she had spent decades growing, holding up the old dollar bill -- the one she had saved from the money Sakolsky had raised. She looked into the camera and said: "Mr. Sakolsky, if you see this video, I invite you to come back to China and see the forest that grew from the money you sent us." The appeal quickly went viral online. Within hours, messages began reaching Sakolsky in the form of emails and texts from strangers telling him that a Chinese woman was looking for him. Less than 26 hours after Yin posted the video, they found him. The two then reconnected online. This was followed by photographs and videos. For the first time, Sakolsky saw what had become of the saplings he had once thought too small to make much difference: a forest of more than 50,000 trees. "Amazing. Absolutely amazing," he said. A DREAM FULFILLED Upon arriving in Beijing early this past Sunday, Sakolsky received mooncakes sent by Yin, a traditional Chinese symbol of reunion, and tomatoes grown in the sandy land. He flew to Ordos that afternoon. "This is a dream come true from a lady who is the hero of the story," he told media gathered around them at the local airport. "I never thought I would see her again," Sakolsky said. For him, this visit brought home the power of a culture that lives by its promises. Yin had vowed that the saplings would take root and grow, and that one day he could come back to see them for himself. Today, including the trees funded by Sakolsky's efforts, Yin and her family have planted trees across 70,000 mu, an area roughly the size of 6,500 standard soccer pitches. Poplars, oriental arborvitaes, spruce and Mongolian Scots pines now rustle in the wind as birds chirp. Official figures show that about 85 percent of the Maowusu has been restored. Between 2021 and 2025, China accounted for roughly one-quarter of the world's increase in green vegetation and managed to rehabilitate approximately 152 million mu of sandified land. When he raised the money in 1999, he expected nothing in return, Sakolsky said. "You can't give something and then expect something back," he told Xinhua. "I raised that money because I wanted to thank China, and I wanted to help her make China a little more beautiful. That's all." On Monday afternoon, Sakolsky walked through a carpet of fallen leaves as Yin led him to a tall, sturdy poplar, more than 10 meters high, in a grove named in his honor. He could hardly believe it. This was the tree he and Yin had planted together 26 years ago. Back then, the sapling had been no thicker than a finger, swaying in the wind as if it might be swallowed by the sand at any moment. Yin handed him a shovel. "Let's plant another one." The two bent down together. Yin steadied the sapling as Sakolsky pressed soil around its roots -- his hands trembling slightly but his movements steady. "I planted a friendship tree in Inner Mongolia," Sakolsky said. FRIENDSHIP FOR GENERATIONS To welcome Sakolsky, more than a dozen members of Yin's family had come from different places to be there for the meeting. Red chili peppers hung by the doorway and small pumpkins lined the walls, while the courtyard had been swept clean. "I asked my children to come back because I hope the friendship between our two families will last for generations," Yin said. "I want my children and grandchildren to remember it." For Sakolsky, the reunion with Yin and her family is about more than a forest. It is a reminder that no act of kindness, no matter how small, is ever wasted. Given time, a small act can take root, spread and grow into something no one could have imagined. The story of Sakolsky and Yin adds another thread to the long history of goodwill between the people of China and the United States -- from the American volunteer pilots who fought alongside Chinese forces during World War II to the historic visit of a U.S. table tennis team to China in 1971 and, more recently, the Philadelphia Orchestra's decades of performances in the country. During his stay in China from Aug. 23 to Sept. 1, Sakolsky will also take part in China-U.S. teacher exchanges and return to Henan, where he will meet teachers and students at the school where he once taught, among other activities. The retired history teacher believes that while people may look different and come from different cultures, underneath it all, everyone bleeds red. "Whether you're Chinese or American, we all love our families, we all love life, and we all love the Earth," he said. Americans and Chinese need to "focus on our similarities and not on our differences," he once noted. He hopes that when the trip is over, the message can reach people around the world: Chinese and American people "can work together and make a peaceful world." "I see where the United States and China can work together," said Sakolsky. "So I will not quit. She never quit. 'Quit' is not in her vocabulary. Together, it works." item.title: 2026 APEC SME ministerial meeting to focus on innovation, cooperation
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-25
2026 APEC SME ministerial meeting to focus on innovation, cooperation A themed installation is pictured at a business district in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province, Aug. 10, 2026. (Xinhua/Liang Xu) BEIJING, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- The 32nd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Small and Medium Enterprises (SME) Ministerial Meeting will be held on Sept. 4 in Guangzhou, south China's Guangdong Province, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) said on Monday. The meeting, themed "innovation-driven development for win-win cooperation," will bring together SME officials from APEC economies, representatives of the APEC Secretariat, and other guests. The meeting will focus on technological innovation, digital empowerment and inclusive development, with a joint ministerial statement and other outcome documents expected, according to Liang Zhifeng, director of the SME bureau under the MIIT. As the host, China hopes that through in-depth exchanges, all economies will reach forward-looking and practical consensus, promote mutual learning of policies and the translation of outcomes, and jointly enhance the innovation capacity, digitalization level and sustainable development capabilities of SMEs in the Asia-Pacific region, said Vice Minister of Industry and Information Technology Ke Jixin. Wang Sheng, vice governor of Guangdong, said that all preparations for the meeting are essentially complete, and all APEC economies had confirmed their participation. More than 2,100 companies from home and abroad have registered for the accompanying exhibitions, with over 3,900 booths planned. China will host the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen in south China in November this year, which will mark the country's third hosting of the event following Shanghai in 2001 and Beijing in 2014. This year marks the APEC "China Year," with the theme of "Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together." Approximately 300 APEC-related meetings and events will take place in multiple Chinese cities throughout the year. Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. All Rights Reserved.

item.title: Xi stresses consolidating, expanding campaign on correct view of governance performance
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-25
Xi stresses consolidating, expanding campaign on correct view of governance performance BEIJING, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- Xi Jinping, general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee, has emphasized the importance of consolidating and expanding the progress made in a Party-wide study and education campaign for establishing and practicing a correct understanding of governance performance. Xi, also Chinese president and chairman of the Central Military Commission, made the remarks in a recent instruction, which was studied at a meeting of the CPC Central Leading Group for Party Building held on Monday. Xi stressed that establishing and putting into practice a correct view of governance performance is a long-term task that requires sustained efforts. Since the 18th CPC National Congress, the organization of study and education campaigns across the Party to address major and pressing issues in Party building has become an important institutional arrangement, Xi said, lauding the notable results achieved in the latest campaign. Xi emphasized the need to regularly conduct education on the correct view of governance performance, guiding Party members and officials to always take responsibility, perform their duties and fulfill their obligations in accordance with such a view. Efforts should also be made to improve differentiated assessment and evaluation systems, and establish a personnel selection and appointment orientation that values solid work and concrete results, Xi said. During the meeting, participants thoroughly studied and implemented Xi's instruction, reviewed the campaign, and made arrangements for consolidating and expanding the campaign's outcomes and establishing a long-term mechanism accordingly. The meeting was chaired by Cai Qi, who is head of the CPC Central Leading Group for Party Building, and was also attended by Li Xi, the group's deputy head. Cai and Li, both of whom are members of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee, also delivered speeches. The meeting noted that the campaign has resolved prominent issues related to deviations in view of governance performance, regulated the official conduct of leading officials at all levels, and given a strong boost to all work aimed at ensuring a good start to the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030). The campaign, which started in late February, has basically concluded and aimed to correct misguided views on governance that often breed vanity projects, hidden risks, heavy burdens on local communities, and public discontent.
